paragraphs: “But how could we not be friendly to you?” said my hostess with a laugh. The room was full of people. Suddenly the young lady stood up, the one the duel had been fought over, the one I had lately meant to marry. I had not seen her come in. She rose, walked over to me and held out her hand.
“I want you to know,” she said, “that I am the first who does not laugh at you. I thank you with tears, and I respect you for what you did that day.”

Her husband came over too, and then they all gathered round me and very nearly kissed me. My heart was full of joy. But one man in particular caught my eye, a man of middle age who had come up with the rest. I knew his name already, yet I had never met him or spoken a word to him before that evening.
_(d) The Mysterious Visitor_

He had held office in our town for many years. His position was a prominent one, everyone respected him, he was rich, and he was known for his kindness. He gave large sums to the almshouse and the orphanage, and he was generous in secret as well, which only came out after he died. He was about fifty, almost stern in appearance, and he did not talk much. He had been married some ten years, and his wife, who was still young, had borne him three children. Well, the next evening I was sitting alone in my room when the door suddenly opened and in walked this gentleman.

I should say, by the way, that I no longer lived in my old lodgings. As soon as I left the army, I rented rooms from an old lady, the widow of a government clerk. Her servant waited on me. The reason I had moved into her house at all was that, coming back from the duel, I had sent Afanasy back to the regiment. After my last talk with him I was ashamed to look him in the face. That is how quick a worldly man is to feel shame at a righteous deed.

“For the last few days,” said my visitor, “I have listened to you with great interest as you spoke in various houses. At last I wanted to meet you in person, so that we might talk more freely. Would you grant me that favor, dear sir?”

“Gladly, with the greatest pleasure. I shall count it an honor.” I said it, though I felt almost dismayed, so deeply did this man impress me from the first moment. Others had listened to me with interest and attention, but nobody had ever come to me looking so serious, so stern and so intent. And now he had come to my own rooms. He sat down.
“I see that you have great strength of character,” he said. “You have dared to serve the truth, even at the risk of everyone’s contempt.”
“You may be praising me too highly,” I replied.

“No, not too highly,” he answered. “Believe me, what you did is much harder than you think. That is what struck me, and that is the only reason I have come to you,” he went on. “Tell me, please, if my curiosity, which may be improper, does not annoy you, what exactly did you feel, if you can remember, at the moment you decided to ask forgiveness at the duel? Do not take my question for an idle one. I have a private reason for asking, which I may explain later, if God wills that we come to know each other better.”
The whole time he spoke, I looked him straight in the face. All at once I felt complete trust in him, and I was very curious too, for I sensed that his soul held some strange secret.

“You ask what exactly I felt when I asked my opponent’s forgiveness,” I answered. “But I had better begin at the beginning, with something I have told no one yet.” And I told him everything that had passed between Afanasy and me, and how I had bowed down at his feet to the ground. “So you can see for yourself,” I concluded, “that at the duel it was easier for me. I had made a start already at home. Once I was on that road, going further along it was not hard at all. It became a source of joy and happiness.”
I liked the way he looked at me while he listened. “All of this,” he said, “is most interesting. I shall come and see you again and again.”

From then on he came to see me almost every evening. We could have become closer friends, if only he had ever spoken of himself. But of himself he said hardly a word, while he never stopped asking about me. Still, I grew very fond of him and talked to him quite openly about all I felt. “For why,” I thought, “should I need to know his secrets, when I can see without them that he is a good man? And grave as he is, and older than I, he still comes to see a youngster like me and treats me as an equal.” I learned a great deal of value from him, for he had a lofty mind.

“That life is heaven,” he said to me suddenly, “is a thought I have turned over for a long time.” Then he added all at once, “In fact, I think of nothing else.” He looked at me and smiled. “I am more sure of it than you are. I will tell you later why.”
I listened and thought that he clearly wanted to tell me something.
“Heaven,” he went on, “lies hidden in every one of us. It lies hidden in me now. If I choose, it will be revealed to me tomorrow and for all time.”
I looked at him. He spoke with deep feeling, and he gazed at me mysteriously, as if he were putting a question to me.

“As for our being all responsible to all and for all, over and above our own sins, you were quite right to think so. It is wonderful that you grasped its whole meaning at once. And truly, once men understand this, the Kingdom of Heaven will be no dream for them but a living reality.”
“And when?” I cried out bitterly. “When will that happen? Will it ever happen? Or is it only a dream of ours?”

“So you do not believe it?” he said. “You preach it and do not believe it yourself. Believe me, this dream, as you call it, will certainly come true. It will come, but not yet, for every process has its law. This is a spiritual, a psychological process. If the world is to be changed and made new, men must first turn to another path in their minds. Until you have truly, in actual fact, become a brother to everyone, brotherhood will not come. No scientific teaching, no common interest, will ever teach men to share property and privilege with the same fairness to all. Everyone will think his share too small. They will always be envying one another, complaining and attacking. You ask when it will come. It will come, but first we must pass through a time of isolation.”
“What do you mean by isolation?” I asked him.

“Why, the isolation that rules everywhere, most of all in our age. It is not yet fully grown. It has not yet reached its limit. Each man strives to hold his individuality as far apart as he can. Each wants the fullest possible life for himself. But all his efforts end not in a fuller life but in self-destruction, because instead of finding himself he ends in utter solitude. In our age all mankind has broken up into separate units. They all keep apart, each in his own rut. Each stands aloof, hiding himself and what he owns from the rest, and he ends by being pushed away by others and pushing them away. He piles up riches alone and thinks, ‘How strong I am now, how safe!’ In his madness he does not see that the more he piles up, the further he sinks into helplessness that destroys him. For he is used to trusting himself alone and to cutting himself off from the whole. He has trained himself not to believe in help from others, from men or from humanity, and he trembles only lest he lose his money and the privileges he has won. In these days, men in their mockery have stopped seeing, everywhere, that real safety lies in standing together with others, not in each one’s lonely effort. But this terrible individualism must come to an end, and suddenly all will see how unnaturally they have been parted from one another. It will be the spirit of the time, and people will be amazed that they sat so long in darkness without seeing the light. And then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in the heavens.... Until then, though, we must keep the banner flying. Sometimes, even if he must do it alone and even if he seems to be acting like a madman, a man has to set an example. He must draw other souls out of their loneliness and rouse them to some act of brotherly love, so that the great idea does not die.”

So our evenings went by, one after another, in this stirring and passionate talk. I gave up society and called on my neighbors far less often. My vogue, besides, was somewhat past. I do not say this to complain, for they still loved me and treated me kindly, but there is no denying that fashion is a mighty power in society. I came to look on my mysterious visitor with admiration. I enjoyed his intelligence, and I also began to see that he was brooding over some plan in his heart and perhaps preparing for a great deed. Perhaps he was pleased that I showed no curiosity about his secret and made no attempt to learn it, by direct question or by hints. But in the end I saw that he seemed to be showing signs of wanting to tell me something. About a month after his first visit this had become quite plain.
“Do you know,” he said to me once, “that the people in town are very inquisitive about us? They wonder why I visit you so often. Let them wonder, for _soon all will be explained_.”

At times a strange agitation would seize him, and nearly always he would then get up and leave. At times he would fix a long, piercing gaze on me, and I would think, “Now he is going to say something.” But he would abruptly start talking about some ordinary, familiar matter. He often complained of headaches too.
One day, with no warning at all, after he had been talking with great fervor for a long time, I saw him turn pale. His face twitched, and he stared hard at me.
“What is it?” I said. “Are you ill?” He had just been complaining of a headache.
“I ... you know ... I murdered someone.”
He said this and smiled, his face white as chalk. “Why is he smiling?” That thought flashed through my mind before I took in anything else. I turned pale too.
“What are you saying?” I cried.
“You see,” he said, with a pale smile, “what it has cost me to say the first word. Now it is said, I feel I have taken the first step, and I shall go on.”

For a long time I could not believe him. I did not believe him then, but only after he had come to me three days running and told me all of it. I thought he was mad, but I ended by being convinced, to my great grief and amazement. His crime was great and terrible.

Fourteen years earlier he had murdered a landowner’s widow, a rich and beautiful young woman who owned a house in our town. He fell passionately in love with her, told her so, and tried to persuade her to marry him. But she had already given her heart to another man, an officer of noble birth and high rank, who was away at the front at that time, though she expected him back soon. She refused his proposal and begged him to stop calling on her. After he had stopped, he used what he knew of the house to slip in one night through the garden and over the roof, at great risk of being caught. But, as often happens, a crime carried out with extraordinary boldness is more likely to succeed than others.

He climbed in through the skylight into the attic and went down the ladder. He knew the door at the foot of it was sometimes left unlocked, because the servants were careless. He hoped to find it so, and he did. In the dark he made his way to her bedroom, where a lamp was burning. As if on purpose, both her maids had gone off, without asking leave, to a birthday party in the same street. The other servants slept in their quarters or in the kitchen on the ground floor. The sight of her asleep set his passion blazing, and then spiteful, jealous rage seized his heart. Like a drunken man, out of his mind, he drove a knife into her heart, so that she did not even cry out. Then, with devilish and criminal cunning, he made sure that suspicion would fall on the servants. He was vile enough to take her purse, to open her chest with keys from under her pillow and take things out of it, doing all this the way some ignorant servant would, leaving valuable papers and taking only money. He took some of the larger gold objects but left smaller things worth ten times as much. He also took a few things for himself as keepsakes, but of that later. When he had done this dreadful deed, he went back the way he had come.

Neither the next day, when the alarm was raised, nor at any time later in his life, did anyone dream of suspecting him. Nobody even knew of his love for her, for he was always reserved and silent and had no friend to whom he would have opened his heart. People saw him merely as an acquaintance of the dead woman, and not a close one, since for the past two weeks he had not even called on her. Suspicion fell at once on one of her serfs, a man called Pyotr, and every circumstance bore it out. The man knew, and his mistress had not hidden it, that she had to send one of her serfs as a recruit and had decided on him, because he had no family and his behavior was poor. People had heard him threaten angrily, drunk in a tavern, to kill her. Two days before her death he had run away and was staying nobody knew where in the town. The day after the murder he was found on the road out of town, dead drunk, with a knife in his pocket, and by chance his right hand was stained with blood. He declared that he had had a nosebleed, but no one believed him. The maids admitted that they had gone to the party and that the street door had stood open until they got back. And a number of similar details came to light, all throwing suspicion on the innocent servant.

They arrested him and he was tried for the murder. But a week after his arrest the prisoner came down with a fever and died, unconscious, in the hospital. There the matter ended. The judges, the authorities and everyone in the town stayed convinced that the crime was the work of the servant who had died in the hospital, and no one else. And after that the punishment began.

My mysterious visitor, now my friend, told me that at first he felt no pangs of conscience whatever. He was wretched for a long time, but not for that reason. He only regretted that he had killed the woman he loved, that she was gone, that by killing her he had killed his love while the fire of passion was still in his veins. Of the innocent blood he had shed, of the murder of a fellow creature, he hardly thought. He could not bear the thought that she might have become another man’s wife, and so for a long time his conscience told him he could not have acted otherwise.

At first the servant’s arrest worried him, but the man’s illness and death soon set his mind at rest. As he reasoned at the time, the man had evidently died not of the arrest or the fright but of a chill caught on the day he ran away, when he lay all night on the damp ground, dead drunk. The theft of the money and other things troubled him little, for he argued that it had been done not for gain but to throw off suspicion. The sum was small, and soon afterwards he donated all of it, and much more, to the fund for keeping up an almshouse in the town. He did this deliberately, to quiet his conscience about the theft, and it is a remarkable fact that for a long time he really was at peace. He told me so himself. Then he threw himself into a career of great activity in the service. He volunteered for a hard and laborious duty that took up two years, and being a man of strong will, he almost forgot the past. Whenever it came back to him, he tried not to think of it at all. He became active in philanthropy as well. He founded and helped support many institutions in the town, did a good deal in the two capitals, and was elected a member of philanthropic societies in both Moscow and Petersburg.
